A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, Table 1, Figure 1, mathematical material, and Appendices A–G support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Appendix A reports an original numerical simulation comparing fixed and adaptive FTRL regularisation across dimensions, with outcomes plotted in Figure 1.

after.justification: Appendix A retains the original FTRL simulation and its reported outcomes in Figure 1.

M1.justification: The adaptive regulariser switch, threshold, and step-size formulas in Section 3 are unchanged, as are the updates in Appendix B and OMD procedures in Appendix G.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic online optimisation scenario using the two-phase loss construction from Appendix E.1. The discussion of translated balls introduces no additional evaluated scenario.

E2.justification: Figure 1 retains the same four methods: FTRL with fixed phi_2, fixed phi_p, adaptive regularisation with the theoretical threshold, and adaptive regularisation with threshold 2d.

E3.justification: Appendix A retains T = 40, L = 1, p = 10, the dimension sweep, regret metric, step sizes, and both switching thresholds. No experimental protocol is added or revised.

E4.justification: The dimension sensitivity and switching-threshold comparison in Appendix A are unchanged. Section 4.4 explains the existing lower-bound construction without adding an ablation, robustness test, or case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars for the simulation. Statistical reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Section 1.2 corrects the stated high-dimensional rate from T^(1/p) to T^(1-1/p), aligning the passage with Table 1 and bounds already present in v1. Figure 1, its four curves, and the experimental findings are unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 explicitly defines coordinatewise sign invariance in footnote 2 and states applicability to translated balls under corresponding regulariser conditions in Remark 4.11. These are limited formal clarifications; the existing bounds and appendix proofs remain unchanged, and Section 4.4 reuses Appendix E.1's construction.

C1.justification: The introduction adds an explicit novelty claim for the fixed-regularisation failure results while acknowledging earlier algorithm-specific lower bounds. The principal anytime-optimality, separable-regulariser impossibility, and bandit lower-bound claims are retained.

C2.justification: New Remark 4.11 discusses a possible connection to quadratically convex sets and conditional applicability to translated balls. Section 4.4 adds a bias–variance interpretation of the existing loss construction, explaining the consequences of small and large step sizes.

D1.justification: Both versions disclose the same implementation information: default Google Colab CPU settings, approximately five minutes of runtime, SciPy minimise with SLSQP for projections, and closed-form updates in Appendix B. No access information or implementation settings change.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gatmiry, Schneider, and Jegelka (2025) to the universality discussion. It also sharpens comparisons with Orabona and Pál's algorithm-specific lower bounds and explains the low-dimensional restriction of the cited Bubeck–Cohen–Li bandit bound.

P1.justification: V2 adds the Proof intuitions subsection, a short applicability remark, and acknowledgments, with limited introduction and conclusion revisions. Cross-reference edits correct two equation references in Appendix E.2 but also incorrectly call several definitions, lemmas, and propositions 'Theorem'.

P2.justification: V2 adds a NeurIPS conference footer and reflows the main text and subsequent pages around the additions. Table 1 retains its structure, and Figure 1 retains the same plot, axes, legend, and caption content apart from an internal-reference wording change.

improvement.justification: Section 4.4 makes the central lower-bound argument easier to follow, and the added prior-work qualifications clarify the contribution. Rate and equation-reference corrections improve accuracy. These limited gains outweigh the introduced cross-reference mislabelling; the substantive proofs and experimental evidence remain stable.
